column2: If this question includes forest entomology the government has carried out a great deal of research work as outlined in reply to question 3.
Forest entomology in B.C.

Yes. In addition to other work of this kind the Dominion Department of Agriculture has paid special attention to injuries by forest insects in British Columbia. For the past six years the division of forest insects of the Dominion entomological branch

column1: has been investigating the extensive forest insect outbreaks in British Columbia. Its officers have studied the insect outbreaks wherever large amounts of timber were being destroyed, have devised and recommended methods of control, wherever possible, and have undertaken the supervision of control measures that were instituted on their recommendations by the provincial forest branch and the Dominion forest service. Through the effect co-operation of these three organizations a large amount of valuable timber has been saved during the past few years.

This work has in the past been devoted chiefly to the control of extensive outbreaks of bark-beetles in yellow pine. The bark-beetle control work has now been brought to a successful conclusion and recently the investigations have been extended to include bark-beetle outbreaks in lodgepole pine, Douglas fir, and other timber trees, injury by the western cedar borer, and other destructive forest insects.

837656,ca.proc.d.1928-04-18.3.2,1928-04-18,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Edmonton):,Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior,YUKON QUARTZ MINING ACT,,,"For regulations I propose to take part of the Ontario statute governing the method by which the computation shall take place for the collection of royalties. We found some little difficulty in applying the provisions of the Ontario law to the Yukon, but since this bill was printed and brought down, I have now a complete set of regulations modelled almost exactly on those contained in the Ontario act, with some very slight changes to make them applicable to the Yukon and also to the three prairie provinces and the Northwest Territories, where I intend to apply this system of the collection of royalties rather than the old system which is now in vogue. I would have no objection to taking the bill out of committee and embodying these regulations in the bill, if that is thought wise by the committee, so that instead of it being left to the minister and the department to make the regulations, they will be a part of the statute. I just wanted to point out to the committee that our difficulty was in making the regulations that are contained in the Ontario act applicable to our conditions. I am prepared now to report progress, so that these regulations may be embodied in the bill.

837674,ca.proc.d.1928-04-18.5.13,1928-04-18,813dc256-6e33-4184-9974-dd19238a9aaf,ca.m.2558,Mr. CARDIN:,Minister of Marine and Fisheries,QUEBEC HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OP $8,500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES",,,"The Quebec harbour commissioners have always contended that the lack of facilities made it impossible for the port to earn sufficient money to meet the interest on the loans made. Up to last year owing to the prohibitive freight rates they were deprived of very important traffic as they were getting no grain shipments over the Transcontinental, although the railway had been built with the view of exporting grain through the port of Quebec. Last year the rates were reduced, and the commissioners expect that they will now be in a position to earn more revenue, and that when the facilities are completed they will be able to meet their obligations. Of this proposed loan of $8,500,000, a little over $2,000,000 is required to increase the storage capacity of the elevator; its present capacity is two million bushels, and this is inadequate. It has been represented that unless additional facilities are provided the port cannot get the benefit of the grain traffic over the Transcontinental which is expected to develop as a result of the reduction of rates.

,Liberal,,Pierre-Joseph-Arthur Cardin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=813dc256-6e33-4184-9974-dd19238a9aaf&Language=E&Section=ALL

Does the minister think there is any probability of the interest being paid in the next twenty-five years? If so, on what does he base his opinion? I think we ought also to have some further information of the nature of the program that warrants this loan so that we may know what is to be done with the money.

written by Mr. Smith, then general manager of the Canadian Co-operative Wheat Producers, Limited, of Winnipeg, under date of October 19, 1927:

I am quite satisfied that to make Quebec a suitable export grain port, you would be forced to increase your present elevator facilities. It is to be remembered your present elevator capacity has to take care of quite a large domestic trade, so that probably only one million bushel capacity is available for export shipment.

This is, of course, quite inadequate, particularly if you ever hope to very materially increase the shipments of grain. With only a million bushel space available, you immediately limit the number of grades a large shipper can send to Quebec, and, as a consequence, your export shipments are curtailed on account of the fact that you only get wheat shipments of one or two grades and in that way miss the steady flow which would naturally result if all types of wheat could be stored at Quebec.
I would therefore strongly recommend to the commissioners at the port of Quebec to increase their present grain elevator capacity by an additional two million bushels.

I am entirely in sympathy with every movement made by the Quebec authorities to develop their port for grain shipments, and believe by the continuance of the efforts already expended you will meet with more success in the near future.

report of the Royal Grain Inquiry Commission of January, 1925:

The situation at Quebec is virtually that of Montreal, with the additional advantage of a longer season. There does not seem to be any reason why the port of Quebec should not share with Montreal a part of the advantages of the St. Lawrence route. Montreal has developed wide business connections with the grain trade so that the traffic is accustomed to move through this port.

It is open to Quebec to do the same thing; no physical obstacles lie in the way of the inauguration of an extensive grain export trade. Indeed, as the capacity of the port of Montreal begins to be taxed at the peak of the movement, a part of the traffic might with advantage move to Quebec. Quebec also enjoys a more favourable insurance rate and is 180 miles nearer to Liverpool than is Montreal.

The report of the special committee of the senate appointed to inquire into the conditions responsible for the routing of large portions of Canadian export grain via American instead of Canadian ports contains the following words:
-that rates be granted upon export grain over the Canadian National railways to Quebec, 56103-1361
Montreal, Halifax. St. John and Vancouver, such as would develop trade through the above ports.
As a corollary to the recommendation in paragraph one, that necessary elevator accommodation should be provided by the Dominion government at Canadian ports.
Recently the chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners, when the board was studying rates, said:

To enable any seaport to handle traffic of this nature (export grain) much outlay must be made, peculiarly and solely adapted to such business. And unless a harbour is equipped for such purpose, it is futile to expect the trade to flow that way.
Commissioner Oliver said:

If sufficient transfer storage, such as exists at Fort William, were provided at Quebec, grain could be moved forward all-rail to that storage at all seasons. During the period of closed navigation it could go into storage (as it now does at Fort William and Port Arthur) to await the opening of navigation on the short ocean haul: and if in storage there, it could be readily pushed forward to St. John and Halifax as required to give return cargo to vessels bringing merchandise to those ports.
I think these opinions are of some importance and are deserving of consideration both by the committee and by the government.

the minister's last argument. I cannot believe that he seriously advances that argument in support of the contention that that will in any way help the revenues of the harbour commissioners of Quebec so that they may be able to pay any modicum of interest on the loans advanced. Let us examine the matter for a minute. The minister suggests that we should increase the capacity of the elevator at Quebec so that grain may be stored there and later forwarded to St. John or Halifax. In the first place the minister argued half an hour ago, and laboured the point, that it was not until they got the rates down this year that they could get grain to Quebec at all. Surely the minister is not going to suggest that this grain from Quebec to St. John is going to be carried free. It certainly is going to pay a heavy freight rate. If the grain is stored all winter or part of the winter in Quebec and then sent on to St. John, it is going to pay the additional rate from Quebec to St. John. How in the name of common sense can the minister expect to move grain through Quebec and on to St. John in that way? Let us take another supposition. Does the minister expect to earn, out of the storage of grain in Quebec, sufficient even to make a showing upon the interest that is going to be charged against it? What are the figures? I am speaking from
Quebec Harbour Commission

memory and am subject to correction, because I am not at all certain of the exactness of my figures, but I think that the normal charge for storage of grain is one cent per bushel per month. Suppose the minister doubles his present bushel capacity of two million bushels; the maximum number of months during which the port would be closed would be five, and he would not expect to carry that grain more than four months, let us say; that would amount to four cents a bushel on two million bushels. It is very easy to figure out what that would amount to; and that is assuming that the elevator was full to capacity, and that there were no difficulties about the different grades of grain. I do not wish to be offensive, but as a matter of fact it is sheer nonsense to suggest that you are going to earn by the storage of grain in Quebec any sum of money that will be commensurate with the needs of the harbour board of that port.

I want to make it perfectly clear that I am out for the development of all the ports of Canada, whether on the Atlantic, the Pacific or the great lakes, where their development can be shown to be a reasonable proposition. I am going to use the port of Vancouver as an illustration. I have under my hand two reports. I sent to the parliamentary library, where certainly all the reports should be available, but all I could get was two, the reports for 1923 and 1924. I am going to show what the port of Vancouver has done in the way of paying interest, and this record has been characteristic of the whole history of the port ever since money was spent there. They set aside, in 1923, $168,000 in the sinking fund, to provide for the retirement of government bonds which were given for advances. They set aside $424,000 for interest during construction of the Ballantyne pier, and they paid to the Dominion government all the interest due on bonds issued, amounting to $145,000.

I take the next year, 1924, and I find that they set aside a reserve for depreciation of $69,000. They paid interest on debentures chargeable to construction amounting to $422,000, and they paid sinking fund reserve amounting to $226,000.

837764,ca.proc.d.1928-04-18.5.103,1928-04-18,7c9ee392-8ed6-4dae-87a9-4c963866732d,ca.m.6222,Mr. LAVIGUEUR:,,QUEBEC HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OP $8,500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES",,,"Mr. Chairman, on

every occasion when we have come before parliament to ask for assistance in developing the port of Quebec we have been told that it is a great national port and should be developed, but the official opposition has always objected that we should first arrange to get' lower grain rates on the Transcontinental railway, and then parliament would be well disposed to vote the money required for this development. Last year we succeeded in obtaining from the railway commission favourable grain rates to the port of Quebec, thus placing it in a position to compete with the other ports of this country. It has been generally recognized that the money so far advanced for the development of the port of Quebec has been well spent not only in the interests of the province and district of Quebec but of Canada as a whole. We are now before parliament asking for an additional sum to continue these works so as to increase the capacity of the grain elevators, which is something that all competent people have admitted for years to be necessary in order to handle properly whatever traffio may go to Quebec. I am greatly surprised, after the arguments that have been advanced in this house for ten or fifteen years to show the necessity for the development of the port of Quebec, that the opposition should offer objection to the undertaking. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite are not serious when they contend that this money is not needed. They cannot be serious when they pretend that the harbour commission of Quebec has not paid interest on its loan. I admit that a part of the interest has not been paid. But, on the other hand, what has the city of Quebec done to justify the expenditure of money to provide improvements necessary for the development of the port? The city of Quebec handed over to the federal government property worth over $5,000,000. What was that for? It was handed over so that the city of Quebec might be given the necessary facilities for its development. This is known to every hon. member of this house and throughout the country. We have a written agreement from the federal government whereby the government under-
Quebec Harbour Commission

takes to do certain works in Quebec to develop that port, in consideration of the property handed over to the federal authorities. When, therefore, hon. members opposite suggest that the commission has not paid interest on the money advanced by the federal government, I say they are not serious, for they overlook the great sacrifice which the citizens of Quebec have made in return for the improvements which they are given. This was recognized by the leader of the Conservative party, Sir Robert Borden himself, who is on record as stating that neither money nor effort should be spared to develop that port. I desire to quote from the first volume of Hansard of the first session of 1919, page 293, what Sir Robert Borden had to say on the subject. As leader of the government at that time, referring to the necessity of our obtaining western traffic, he said:

Having regard to the probable enormous development of western traffic to this city and its wonderful possibility by reason of the situation which I have described and seeing also the necessity of providing adequately for future development, the government thought it desirable to possess an extensive waterfront on the St. Lawrence. With this view we have acquired three miles of the best waterfront in Quebec extending from Sillery to Cap Diamond; and portions of the waterfront from the Cap Diamond to the Champlain market have also been secured. This magnificent waterfront will give to the government and to the harbour commission the opportunity of almost unlimited development of port and terminal facilities; and 1 hope you will agree that in thus looking forward to the possibilities of the future the government have taken no unwise course. In adopting -this policy, we feel that we are acting not in the interest of Quebec alone but in the interest of all Canada, for Canada as a whole is concerned in the provision of modern and effective facilities necessary for the outflow and inflow' of commerce at all great ports.

Those are the words of the leader of the government of that day who recognized that the port of Quebec had to be developed at all costs. It is nothing new to members from Quebec to see such strong opposition when we come before parliament asking, not for charity or for any favours, but that we be given what is our due. We vote millions of money for the development of the harbour of Toronto and other ports as well, and no opposition is offered when reasonable explanations are given for these expenditures. But every time we come before parliament asking for money for the port or the city of Quebec, there is always this opposition, as though we were asking for charity. Once more I say we are not asking for charity, because in return for what we receive we have surrendered to the government more than any other city of Canada has given.

,Liberal,,Henri-Edgar Lavigueur,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=7c9ee392-8ed6-4dae-87a9-4c963866732d&Language=E&Section=ALL
837765,ca.proc.d.1928-04-18.5.104,1928-04-18,6d54c06b-83db-41ad-8ccf-5ad09a81d62a,ca.m.5750,Mr. BRADY:,,QUEBEC HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OP $8,500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES",,,"I rise to protest against what I consider, in view of the facts we have before us, a very unnecessary expenditure involving a vast sum of money, particularly under conditions that do not by any means substantiate the claims that are being made therefor. I happen to have a few facts which I should like to present to the committee and particularly to the members of the prairie provinces regarding precisely the relationship of the port of Quebec to the prairies. We find that the prairie grain area extends about 900 miles west of Winnipeg; that is to say that grain shipped from west of Winnipeg to Fort William is hauled over 1,250 miles. The average haul of grain reaching Fort William is approximately 800 miles. Taking the several grain railway points some 400 miles west of Winnipeg as the centre of grain production, the average length of haul to Quebec would be 1,750 miles, which is double the length of haul from Winnipeg to Fort William. We know there are three routes by which grain moves from the western provinces; one is by lake and canal, the second is by lake and rail and the third all-rail, which is the way I believe grain would come from the prairies to the port of Quebec. I find that the Board of Railway Commissioners have said that the lake and canal route is fundamentally cheaper and better than the all-rail route; in fact they say the all-rail route is practically ignored as compared with the other two routes. The evidence given by both railways was that their respective western equipments and organizations were fully employed only during one-third of the year while the grain movement was greatest between harvest and the close of navigation on the lakes, and that during the remainder of the year two-thirds of their equipment was idle and their organizations disrupted for lack of traffic. Moreover, we find that the development of this port to such an extent seems to be contrary to the development of our waterways about which we have heard so much, this session, and I fail to see how this great expenditure at Quebec is in agreement with the data which we have received with regard to the hauling of grain.

We are all great advocates of the development of Canadian ports; that is a fundamental principle to which I think we will all agree, and just here I would like to refer to perhaps the newest port on the Pacific coast. We have heard about Vancouver, which is a splendid port and a city with a great future, but the port of Prince Rupert is conceded to be a second Portsmouth. During- all seasons of the year, by day and by night, vessels can enter that harbour from two directions, from the north of the Queen
Quebec Harbour Commission

Charlotte Islands or from the south by Cape St. James. There are no tides to interfere with the movement of vessels; there are no fogs to hamper shipping, and along the inner harbour for a distance of eight miles the depth of water is not less than forty feet along the waterfront. The future of the Pacific coast is assured; the great developments in shipping will be on the Pacific, and what is this government doing to promote the great oriental trade which must be developed by either Canada or the United States? The number of vessels entering Prince Rupert has increased since the elevator was built, and we must attribute to the Alberta wheat pool the movement of grain to that port, they have recognized its strategic position and have increased the movement of grain in that direction. Up until last week I think twenty-eight ocean going vessels called at that port, and while I do not know the amount of grain which will go through it this year, I presume it will be in the neighbourhood of 10,000,000 bushels. Last year, which was the first year grain was shipped through Prince Rupert, about 6,000,000 bushels passed through that port. So I would point out that this huge expenditure at Quebec, when all the facts are opposed to it, cannot be in the public interest and certainly is not for the well being of Canada at large. Therefore I do protest against such a large amount of money being spent upon a harbour which during 1926, exported only 3,095,334 bushels of grain, while the port of Montreal exported 74,660,253 bushels during the same period. I can hardly believe the object of this expenditure is to take trade away from Montreal; for I do not believe the exportation of grain from Quebec will be greatly increased by building immense terminals at that port. Even if two elevators are constructed there I do not believe the volume of grain passing through Quebec will be greatly increased.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,James Charles Brady,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6d54c06b-83db-41ad-8ccf-5ad09a81d62a&Language=E&Section=ALL
837766,ca.proc.d.1928-04-18.5.105,1928-04-18,c2394337-f8ed-4555-877d-cc6d79e6700e,ca.m.5981,Mr. EVANS:,,QUEBEC HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OP $8,500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES",,,"It is said that the purpose

for which this motion is brought before the house at this time is to facilitate the shipping of western grain to the markets of the world, and since I have been in this parliament it has been said repeatedly that these great expenditures on the ports of eastern Canada have been made for the benefit of the western farmer. It seems to me that there is no doubt that the port of Quebec has been discriminated against, and during the last few years it has come out several times in this house that this discrimination has been practised by a combination of shipping companies and by the insurance companies. To such
an extent has this been the case that demurrage has been charged for the time taken by a boat to go from Montreal to Quebec to load grain.

Too many of these expenditures are made on the excuse that they are for the benefit of the western farmers; the new elevator at Halifax is another sample of that sort of thing, and it is all charged up against the grain trade. In my opinion, unless Quebec can be shown as a point where package freight will be loaded to the extent to which this improvement will be needed, this expenditure should not be made. I do not believe Quebec will ever be a very great port with regard to the shipment of grain. In the west a good many years ago the Saskatchewan Co-operative Elevator Company found it necessary to construct a large terminal at Buffalo. The grain landed at Buffalo is within ten or twelve hours of a port that is open all the year round. At ports such as New York and Boston bargains can be made and transportation secured at the very lowest price. We have found out during the last twenty years, when the Transcontinental has been in use, that the port of Quebec is not a grain port. I think this tremendous sum of money which the house is asked to vote for the port of Quebec is unwarranted and unnecessary. I wish to protest against it and I do so for the reason that the facilities already existing at Quebec have never been used to their fullest capacity, and this is particularly the case in regard to grain. When this expenditure is shown to be necessary I am sure the country will make the necessary appropriation, but at present I am opposed to it and cannot do less than vote against the resolution.

837767,ca.proc.d.1928-04-18.5.106,1928-04-18,06b3ede1-7cd7-46e9-87f5-23c426b95e96,ca.m.4681,Mr. CAMPBELL:,,QUEBEC HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OP $8,500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES",,,"When a vote of $5,000,000 for the purpose of increasing the facilities at the port of Quebec was proposed in 1925 the group in this corner of the house strenuously opposed it. We pointed out in substance that every facility should be provided for developing trade through that port, but the existing facilities should be fully taken advantage of before further expenditures were made. It is true that since that time the discrimination in freight rates against the port of Quebec have been removed. That, perhaps, is the argument used by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to-day in asking that a further sum of money be voted to increase the facilities of that port. To that extent I am with the minister. I believe there is an opportunity now of developing a considerable amount of trade through that port. I do not agree that the rate of 11 cents a bushel from
Quebec Harbour Commission

Armstrong to Quebec is an entirely prohibitive one. It is true that it is higher than the usual rate paid on the lakes; but in the early spring and summer, when the full movement of grain is on and there is a lack of competition amongst the vessels moving the grain, the grain rates on the lakes have frequently been higher than 11 cents a bushel. In fact, on one occasion, I think it was in 1922, we paid an average rate of 14 cents on the lakes during the whole season, three cents higher than the present rate to Quebec. Now that the rate to that port has been reduced to 11 cents I believe it will set a maximum for lake and rail traffic. I believe the steamship companies will keep their rates down to 11 cents, so that the reduced rate to Quebec has had a very good effect in that respect. I believe that at certain times in the year, particularly after the lake ports close in the fall, a considerable amount of grain will move forward to Quebec. In addition to that I am of the opinion that there will be opportunities of developing the cattle trade, provided that our cattle do not continue to go to the United States as they do at present. I think we shall develop not only a cattle trade, but traffic in other lines, to the port of Quebec. We in this group kept consistently hammering at the rate question for four or five years until something was finally accomplished. We can hardly be accused therefore of trying to divert the shipment of our own products to foreign ports. It has been proved conclusively that our grain deteriorates in quality when it passes through United States ports. If one will read the report of Professor Rutherford, which is attached as an appendix to the report of the Royal Grain Commission of 1923, it will be found that he points out, as the result of his investigations in the old country, that grain carrying a Canadian grade certificate and arriving in the old country from United States ports has a lower grade than Canadian certified grain shipped from Canadian ports. It shows conclusively that although this grain carries a Canadian grade certificate it is mixed when it passes in transit through the United States, a fact which is seriously affecting the marketing of our grain to-day. Professor Rutherford also points out that in the case of grain arriving in the old country from Vancouver the Canadian grade certificate is accepted due to the fact that there is no mixing at the port in question, or there was none at the time. Therefore it is to our interests to see that every bushel of grain possible is carried through Canadian ports, and I am prepared to go a long way to assist the government in bringing about that condition of affairs.

I am sorry that we have not a little more information on this matter. In view of the fact that $5,000,000 was spent on Quebec only three years ago it is hardly reasonable to expect the house to vote this large amount of extra money now. On the other hand I think that if we could be assured that these facilities were really necessary and that there was going to be sufficient trade at Quebec in a few years to take advantage of them, no objection to the vote would be raised in this part of the house. I suggest that the minister send this resolution to a committee. If that were done there could be called before the committee members of the harbour commission of the port of Quebec, members of the wheat pool, representatives of shipping companies and other interests and the whole matter could be thoroughly investigated. I am sure that we are fair enough not to offer any opposition to the vote provided that the necessity of these facilities is fully demonstrated. But with the information at present in our possession I am not convinced that this expenditure is necessary, and in view of the fact that the port of Quebec has not been paying even interest on its bonds, it is unreasonable to exipect this house1 to vote such a very large sum of money without at least having before it some further information. I am not one of those who hold the Quebec harbour commission responsible for the condition of affairs in the past, because we have been lending the commission money on the one hand to provide facilities, and on the other hand dteliberately preventing trade from going to that port. That is the condition of affairs that has existed in the past, due to the prohibitive rates that have existed on the Transcontinental.

The minister of Marine and Fisheries made a statement some little time ago, which was reported in the press, to the effedt that if the insurance companies did not cease to discriminate against the ports of Quebec and Montreal, he proposed to see that a Canadian Lloyd's was established. I congratulate the minister upon making that statement, and I hope the matter will not be allowed to remain there. It is something that some of us in this section of the house have been suggesting for many years-not that there should be a Canadian Lloyd's in its entirety, I do not agree with that; but that a large insurance corporation, centralized we shall say at Montreal, as it likely would be, would be of very considerable assistance. I do not believe a profit-making institution, existing purely bo pay dividends, would bring any large measure of relief. What we have in the past suggested to the government is that they build up an organization similar to what
Quebec Harbour Commission

exists within the Canadian National Railways to-day, an institution that would insure cargoes from all our Canadian ports, collect the regular rate of marine insurance and refund at the end of the year all the money left in the treasury. This institution should be in the hands of capable business men who would see that it was efficiently managed and operated on a 'CokLblaoded business basis, and if the money on hand at the end of the year over and above operating expenses were refunded to the shippers of all those goods, I believe we would then eliminate all the discrimination against Canadian ports. That is where a good deal of the trouble exists to-day, and I suggest to the minister that he consider the establishment of some such organization.

There is no doubt in my mind that shipments from Quebec should carry a very much lower rate of insurance than shipments from Montreal. I have been assured that at least two-thirds of the risk between Montreal and Liverpool is based on the risk in the St. Lawrence river alone, so that the insurance rate from Quebec ought to be relatively smaller than that from Montreal. Under present conditions, however, we are not likely to have a lower rate, for the simple reason that not merely Lloyds but any organization we might build up here would very likely have its headquarters in Montreal, and it is hardly reasonable to expect that a business organization of that kind would do otherwise than endeavour, so far as possible, to assist shipments from their own port. This is the particular business of the government, and if the government really want to assist the movement of traffic to Quebec, I earnestly suggest to the minister that he take the matter into consideration and try to build up an organization along that line. This is not a new experiment; it is done already by the Canadian National Railways and by the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The minister knows, as does every member of the house, that millions of dollars have been saved to the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Government Merchant Marine by that system of handling their own insurance.

Unpaid interest on the foregoing loans, calculated to December 31, 1926, $8,830,992.52.

837851,ca.proc.d.1928-04-18.5.190,1928-04-18,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUEBEC HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OP $8,500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES",,,"I suggest that the government should endeavour to adjust these claims: before we proceed further with this resolution. In my opinion the harbour commission of Quebec have a correct and proper claim against the other departments of the government if their wharves have been used by those departments and if they have not been paid for such use. That is my personal opinion as a lawyer, because it is quite clear that the space thus utilized cost the harbour commission money upon which they have been paying interest. That is quite clear from the report which has been tabled here. The question now is as to the fair allowance for
Quebec Harbour Commission

the use of that space and the interest which should be allowed for the non-payment of these rentals by the government departments. There is the further point that it is unfair to ask the harbour commission to pay interest if we do not allow them interest if they are entitled to anything. We all want to be fair, and in my judgment this matter should be adjusted without delay, because we are carrying $8,800,000 arrears of interest against the harbour commission of Quebec, against which they say they have a set-off amounting to many millions of dollars. I do suggest to the Minister of Finance and to the various departments affected that this matter be adjusted without further delay, and the whole debenture debt of the harbour commission reorganized in some way. This might be done as my hon. friend from Centre Vancouver has suggested, by issuing new debentures indicating the amount of the indebtedness as of January 1, 1928. There is nothing more conducive to this very condition than to continue this sort of thing, which is not right or proper. If the facilities which cost the Quebec harbour commission a large amount of money have been used by another department without payment, the commission have been deprived of that space which might or might not have been used by someone else, and they are entitled to receive a reasonable rental.

Here is another difficulty which I think the government might also consider. This is a large sum of money and, when I saw this resolution on the order paper I proceeded to make certain inquiries. We are asked to grant $8,500,000 to the harbour commissioners, and this amount represents 50 per cent of the money which has been expended there so far. That must be borne in mind. Now I find that the large liners are being constructed in such a way as will permit them to go to Montreal, and we are spending roughly $1,500,000 a year to make it possible to navigate from Montreal to Quebec. For instance, the new ships Laurentie and Megantic, together with the new Duchess ships of the Canadian Pacific line, are going to Montreal. I only learned that last week, in consequence of inquiries which I made after I saw this resolution on the order paper. I understand that additional beam has been provided so that the depth of water required will be somewhat less than was formely the case, and the large liners, including the Duchess of Athol and the Duchess of Bedford, as well as the Laurentie and Megantic, ships of roughly 20,000 tons register, all go to Montreal. Under these circumstances, might it not be desirable

for the minister to reconsider this resolution, first to give effect to the very proper claims of the Quebec harbour commissioners for such sums as may represent a just and proper rental for the use of their facilities by the various departments of the government? In that regard this is no different from railway companies, which have inter-departmental charges. When one department uses the telegraph system, for instance, although it may have a frank, a charge is made for that particular service. The same applies to other branches of industry; the manufacturing end of a concern makes a charge against the administrative end if it uses part of the manufactured material of that concern, and this is exactly the same principle. The harbour commissioners have only one thing to sell; they sell space, and if that space is used by some of the departments of the government a fair rental should be paid.

Then I submit to the minister that in view of the sums which we are compelled to pay annually to maintain and extend the channel between Montreal and Quebec, and having regard to the fact that these large ships now proceed to Montreal, it is desirable to reconsider the whole situation as to whether or not at this moment it is desirable to contemplate such a large expenditure. This is a national port; I need hardly say that this is not a Quebec port in the general sense of that term. This is a national port and is the concern of every part of Canada, perhaps more especially western Canada because the facilities with respect to grain are the facilities from which it is expected a very large revenue will be obtained if those facilities are used by the public to their full extent. 837856,ca.proc.d.1928-04-18.5.195,1928-04-18,3c716a03-43b1-401d-820f-7921b10e5565,ca.m.6937,Mr. ROBB:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,QUEBEC HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OP $8,500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES",,,"If it is not compounded in the one case it is not in the other, and both accounts are on the same basis. And then it

must be remembered that they have an overdraft in the bank amounting to some $747,000 odd. But coming back to the question of expenditure, the Dominion of Canada has advanced the sum of $14,000,000 to provide facilities at the port of Quebec where large liners call. If we did not make provision for the accommodation there of these large steamships their passengers would probably go to New York, Boston, or some other port in the United States, because they would not go by vessel to Montreal. My hon. friend will agree that most of the first class passengers disembark at Quebec and take the train there to their destination. We must keep in mind that we are bringing business to our Canadian railways, and it is not all Canadian business. I recall coming home on a vessel last year that was loaded down, every berth occupied, and on the whole ship there were not one hundred Canadians; most of the passengers were on their way to the middle west and other parts of the United States. That represents the business we are getting through the great port of Quebec. If you compare the $14,000,000 we have invested in Quebec with the money spent on inland ports by the Department of Public Works, I think the comparison will not be disadvantageous to the port of Quebec. My hon. friends might very well allow the resolution to go through, and then the bill to be founded on it can be introduced.
